data.name: Benchmark_Intro
data.value:
The test compares GPU and CPU decoding, drawing the overlay with and without shadows, and transferring frames and encoding in FFmpeg. It also measures the complete FFmpeg pipeline, performs a short render and measures how smoothly the preview plays, both in this window and in the app's player. Everything is shown live. Finally, it identifies the slowest stage and suggests faster settings.
Each comparison alternates between the options over multiple runs. Results show the median and range of measurements. The test takes 3-4 minutes. Close games and other programs that heavily use the CPU or GPU during the test.

data.value: The receiver, available satellites, and surroundings. The same receiver may work well in an open area and less accurately between tall buildings or under trees.

data.name: Calibration_FaqObstaclesQuestion
data.value: What causes jumps in position and speed?

data.name: Calibration_FaqObstaclesAnswer
data.value: Weak signals and reflections from buildings can cause incorrect readings. In a tunnel, the receiver may lose the signal entirely. Wait for the receiver to establish its position before you start riding.

data.name: Calibration_FaqSpeedQuestion
data.value: Does position accuracy determine speed accuracy?

data.name: Calibration_FaqSpeedAnswer
data.value: No. Knowing that position is accurate within a few meters does not tell you the speed error in km/h. The accuracy of each measurement is assessed separately.

data.name: Calibration_FaqReferenceQuestion
data.value: How should I choose a speed correction?

data.name: Calibration_FaqReferenceAnswer
data.value: Example: while driving at a steady speed, the car's speedometer reads 50 km/h and GPS reads 46 km/h. If you use the speedometer as your reference, enter 50 in the reference speed field and 46 in the GPS reading field. The app will calculate an 8.6% correction. Compare the readings in several parts of the recording instead of relying on a single peak.

data.name: Calibration_FaqLimitsQuestion
data.value: What does correction change in OsmoOverlay?

data.name: Calibration_FaqLimitsAnswer
data.value: In this example, an 8.6% correction raises the GPS reading from 46 km/h to about 50 km/h. It applies to speeds on the overlay; distance, route, and lean stay the same. It does not remove GPS errors or reduce readings that are too high.

data.name: Calibration_FaqCivilianQuestion
data.value: Is civilian GPS deliberately made less accurate?

data.name: Calibration_FaqCivilianAnswer
data.value: No. Deliberate degradation of civilian GPS accuracy ended in May 2000. Today's measurement errors are not caused by that restriction.

data.name: Benchmark_TestRecordingContents
data.value: The test recording is three 10-second 4K 59.94 fps files in 10-bit HEVC, split the way a camera splits them. The picture is deliberately hard: film grain, a zone plate, a fractal, a fast pan, scene cuts and flashes. The stream has B-frames, irregular keyframes, a variable bitrate, a frozen stretch and a dropped frame. At the joins the sound runs longer than the picture, and the third file starts after the camera was stopped. The telemetry is a ride along field roads at up to 150 km/h: no GPS fix or time at the start, a wandering position while standing, jolts, a GPS loss at full speed, a position jump, hard braking before a corner, a lean and a dip in the ground. The first time, the recording is generated (under a minute on a graphics card, a few minutes on the CPU) and kept in the app's data folder (about 360 MB).
